the_ruling_verbatim: Stub them at sys.modules like litellm
now_the_spec_says: aider_shim's venv holds the measured import-time set MINUS litellm, and the shim pre-empts sys.modules for three names, not one: litellm, posthog, mixpanel. Absence, not a flag, is what stops each — so a failed interception raises ImportError instead of dialing out.
the_reason_that_dies: No file dies. What dies is a reflex that was the cheap pick on the table: install the full upstream requirement set and rely on aider's own --analytics-disable flag and its opt-in gate. That is a disposition living in the foreign program's code, re-decided by every upgrade of it and invisible to us when it changes. The ruling replaces it with a construction we own. The lesson generalises past this device: when a hazard's mitigation can be either 'their flag is set the way we hope' or 'the package is not on disk', the second is the one that survives an upgrade nobody watched.
context: THE OMISSION CONVERTS THE FENCE FROM AN INTERCEPTION INTO A PHYSICS. With litellm absent from the venv, the one way the interception could be bypassed — a failure of install ordering — raises ImportError at aider's first exception construction rather than quietly loading a real provider client. The fence stops depending on our code running first and starts depending on a package not being there (Law 4). This is legal only because it is MEASURED: an AST closure over aider's import graph (60 aider modules, 24 third-party roots) put litellm in the lazy-only set beside bs4, httpx, jsonschema, llama_index, networkx and playwright — aider never imports it at startup, and LazyLiteLLM exists precisely because upstream wanted that. The telemetry stub is the same mechanism on the same kind of hazard: posthog and mixpanel load at aider IMPORT time via aider/analytics.py, so holding aider in-process puts two telemetry clients in a Cairn process; stubbed, they cannot transmit because they do not exist. RULED at the piece the build deliberately stopped in front of. The triage berth had ordered the runnable aider FOURTH — after the interceptor and after the money-fence — because every ordering that installs a runnable agentic program before the fence exists opens a window in which the thing that wants to dial providers is present and the thing that would refuse it is a plan. The build honoured that order, committed pieces 2 and 3 proved (12 mutants injected, 12 killed), and escalated rather than proceeding under an assumption: it is the only piece that changes the box rather than the repo. Both answers came back stronger than the options ranked first, and that is the pattern worth keeping — the recommended option in each pair was the one matching upstream's expectations, and he took the one that removed the dependency instead.
